extracted.intended_audience: linguistics/pragmatics researchers and students analysing humour and stand-up performance
extracted.subtask_description: Use formal semantics, Gricean pragmatics, and Austinian performatives to analyse jokes and comedic performance (example subject: Bo Burnham). Includes selection/transcription, ontology construction, categorisation of comedic devices, and pragmatic/performative analysis.

rubrics_metrics.name: Cooperative Principle (overall)
rubrics_metrics.description: Make your conversational contribution such as is required, at the state at which it occurs, by the accepted purpose or direction of the talk exchange in which you are engaged (Grice, 1995:26).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Treat the principle as an axiom/guideline for conversation, contractual in nature: participants rely on mutual adherence for efficient exchanges. It is a set of guidelines, not absolute rules; cultural variation and vagueness mean maxims can be interpreted differently. Useful as a baseline assumption when attributing conversational implicatures.

rubrics_metrics.name: Maxim: Quantity
rubrics_metrics.description: 1) Make your contribution as informative as is required (for the current purpose of the exchange). 2) Do not make your contribution more informative than is required.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluate whether a speaker supplies too little or too much information given the conversational goal. Example: giving an unnecessary detail ('γ has not yet been to prison') may violate one or both submaxims. Consider context and whether extra information is relevant to the interlocutor's needs.

rubrics_metrics.name: Maxim: Quality
rubrics_metrics.description: Try to make your contribution one that is true. Submaxims: 1) Do not say what you believe to be false. 2) Do not say that for which you lack adequate evidence.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assess veracity and evidential support for assertions. In analysis, note when a joke's literal claim lacks evidence (possible flouting) or when falsehoods are knowingly presented for effect (irony, hyperbole). Cultural/contextual ambiguity (e.g. speaker belief vs. actual truth) complicates strict application.

rubrics_metrics.name: Maxim: Relation
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Judge whether contributions are appropriately related to the prior discourse or task. Apparent irrelevance can signal implicature (speaker implies something about character or situation) or be part of comedic technique (misdirection, non sequitur).

rubrics_metrics.name: Maxim: Manner
rubrics_metrics.description: Be clear in how you say things: 1) Avoid obscurity of expression. 2) Avoid ambiguity. 3) Be brief (avoid unnecessary prolixity). 4) Be orderly.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Analyse delivery features (tone, sarcasm, brevity, order) as they affect interpretation. Example: same words uttered sarcastically vs. neutrally lead to different meanings. 'Be orderly' can be extended to politeness/social norms; submaxims are vague and context-sensitive.

rubrics_metrics.name: Conditions for claiming a conversational implicature
rubrics_metrics.description: A person who, by saying that p has implicated that q, conversationally implicated q provided: (1) the speaker is at least to some extent following the maxims/Cooperative Principle; (2) supposing they believe q is required to make their saying p consistent with that presumption; (3) the speaker thinks the listener can work out that the supposition is required (Grice).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use these three checks when attributing implicature: verify assumed cooperative behaviour, infer what belief would render the utterance coherent, and assess whether the listener can reasonably recover that inference. Applied in humour analysis to detect intended indirect meanings.

rubrics_metrics.name: Requirements for a listener to 'work out' a conversational implicature
rubrics_metrics.description: A listener must rely on: (1) conventional meanings and references, (2) the Cooperative Principle and its maxims, (3) the utterance context (linguistic or other), (4) background knowledge, and (5) that the relevant information (1–4) is available to all parties and known to be available (Grice: five points).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When analysing jokes, check each of these five information sources to see whether the audience can compute implicatures. Failure in any can block implicature or change its content (e.g., language barrier, asymmetric knowledge).

rubrics_metrics.name: Types of meaning to consider
rubrics_metrics.description: Four types of meaning: (1) timeless meaning(s) of an utterance-type (complete/incomplete); (2) applied timeless meaning(s) (complete/incomplete); (3) occasion-meaning (context-linked); (4) the utterer's occasion-meaning (what the utterer intends by the utterance).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Distinguish between what an utterance-type can mean in general, what it means in this application, the context-specific meaning, and the speaker's intended meaning. Examples: 'Albert is dying' can mean literally dying, laughing, embarrassed depending on type and context; use these categories to separate possible readings in humour analysis.

rubrics_metrics.name: Austinian felicity conditions for performatives
rubrics_metrics.description: For a performative utterance to be 'happy' (successfully executed), the following must hold: A.1 an accepted conventional procedure with conventional effect must exist (words by certain persons in certain circumstances); A.2 the persons/circumstances must be appropriate; B.1 the procedure must be executed correctly; B.2 completely; C.1 participants must have required thoughts/feelings and intend consequent conduct; C.2 must actually so conduct themselves subsequently (Austin 1962:14–15).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use these conditions to judge whether a performative (e.g., promise, bet, naming) succeeds, is misinvoked (A failure), misexecuted (B failure), or abusive/insincere (C failure). Example: a naming ceremony where wrong person speaks = misinvocation; smashing bottle on ground = misexecution; sincere words but wrong intentions = abuse.

rubrics_metrics.name: Categories of locutionary acts
rubrics_metrics.description: A locutionary act comprises: 1) the phonetic act (uttering noises); 2) the phatic act (noises belong to vocabulary and grammar); 3) the rhetic act (uttering with definite sense and reference).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Break down utterances into these components when analysing meaning and force. Example: 'It is snowing' as phonetic/phatic; asserting 'α says it is snowing' as rhetic. Note that identical phatic acts may yield different rhetic acts depending on context and nuance.

rubrics_metrics.name: Illocutionary vs perlocutionary acts
rubrics_metrics.description: Illocutionary acts are the way a locutionary act is used (asking, warning, announcing, etc.). Perlocutionary acts are the effects produced on listeners (feelings, thoughts, actions).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Identify the illocutionary force (speaker's conventional function) and intended perlocution (the effect sought). In humour, a locution may function as warning, statement, or joke; the perlocution might be to make the audience laugh. Context determines force.

rubrics_metrics.name: Dikkers' eleven joke categories
rubrics_metrics.description: Eleven heuristic categories for classifying jokes: (1) irony, (2) character, (3) reference, (4) shock, (5) parody, (6) hyperbole, (7) wordplay, (8) analogy, (9) madcap, (10) meta-humor, (11) misplaced focus (Dikkers/TheOnion).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use these categories as analytical tools (not exclusive labels). A joke may instantiate multiple categories. The paper uses these to assign comedic devices before semantic/performative analysis.

rubrics_metrics.name: Four-step procedure for joke analysis
rubrics_metrics.description: Procedure: (1) assign one or more comedic categories to a joke; (2) identify and create the ontology per the formal semantics/model theory; (3) identify and categorize performatives (Austin); (4) identify and analyse utterer’s intention and meaning via Grice's Cooperative Principle and maxims.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Follow these steps sequentially for each selected joke. Notes: the paper assumes, for analytic purposes, that Bo Burnham and audience by default follow the Cooperative Principle. Steps (2) and (4) are highlighted as problematic—ontologies may change little across jokes and intention is often simply 'to make the audience laugh', so analysis must dig deeper into submeanings and apparatus of performance.

rubrics_metrics.name: Real ontology vs imaginary ontology (ontology construction guideline)
rubrics_metrics.description: Define for a state-of-affairs S: ORe_S (real ontology) and OIm_S (imaginary ontology). Real ontology = actual participants/objects; imaginary ontology = people/objects in recounted or fictional story. Imaginary ontology is treated as a subset of the state-of-affairs for analysis purposes.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When modelling jokes, explicitly separate elements that belong to the performance's real world (performer, audience, physical props) and the story-world invoked by the joke. Provide explanations for predicates when liberties are taken in the formal model. The imaginary ontology often carries more analytic substance in storytelling jokes.

rubrics_metrics.name: Data selection and subject-choice criteria
rubrics_metrics.description: Choose comedians and jokes to maximise analytic payoff: select subjects with diverse 'schtick' (comedic type and comedic force), choose shows containing visual/personal elements (one-man shows preferred for undiluted voice), and pick jokes diverse in performance and content.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Rationale: Bo Burnham chosen for blending musical acts, storytelling, and physical performance (versatility). Use shows rather than albums/films for richer visual and personal content. Select jokes across types (songs, stories) to capture range. Document selection rationale and limitations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Methodological stance: qualitative approach and its limits
rubrics_metrics.description: Adopt a qualitative approach to gain deep insight into how a comedian constructs comedy; acknowledges that small sample limits generalisability about a performer's overall 'type' or 'force'.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use qualitative analysis for in-depth case study; if claiming the comedian's 'real' comedic type/force, prefer quantitative expansion (larger sample). Be explicit about analytic scope and do not overgeneralise from a limited set.

rubrics_metrics.name: Analytic assumption about cooperative behaviour in performance
rubrics_metrics.description: For analytical purposes in this paper, treat the utterer (Bo Burnham) and the audience as following the Cooperative Principle and maxims by default.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This simplifying assumption allows focus on mechanisms of humour (implicature, performative felicity, ontology) rather than basic conversational failure. When evidence suggests deliberate flouting (e.g., for comic effect), mark and analyse that as a tactic rather than as noise.
